
=================================================================
#41 Suro  (42)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Chunchu Era · place: geumgwan · tone: founder fairy tale
Logline: Before there is a Gaya, there is a ridge, and a sky god who looks at it too long.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Before there is a Gaya, there is a ridge, and a sky god who looks at it too long.
[1] ¶ **Ibiga** keeps the sky the way other gods keep a hall — cloud is his body, the living world a map he does not usually read. Then he looks down.
[2] [CARD Ibiga: The sky god. Cloud is his body, and he does not usually look down.]
[3] ¶ On her mountain the Lady of the Right View is on watch. At first she is the ridge — jade stone, mist, a woman’s shape the mountain has not admitted yet. The mountain is a woman before it has a face. Then a face comes out of the stone. She is guarding the mountain as if it were a country. She does not look up. She does not need to. Then the sky occupies the path. Cloud comes down to the ridge.
[4] [CARD Lady of the Right View: The mountain goddess. The ridge was a woman before anyone noticed.]
[5] Ibiga: That ridge… / That woman. / I have flown this path a thousand times. Why is the mountain looking back.
[6] ¶ Love arrives as weather — sudden, unasked. He cannot keep the hour. He falls before he lands. The sky comes down to touch the mountain, and does not leave.
[7] Ibiga: Mountain. / Your shoulder… is warmer than cloud. / Your waist… steeper than cliff.
[8] Lady of the Right View: Why has heaven come down. / To look? / Or… to touch. / If to touch… kneel first.
[9] Ibiga: To touch. / I looked… and could not hold back. / The knees… already are.
[10] Lady of the Right View: Then closer. / Ridges do not keep guests long. / Tonight I will make an exception. / I will keep your mouth… at my throat.
[11] Ibiga: Your name… Right View. / The longer I look, the less rightful my thoughts become. / I want to put heaven… between your thighs.
[12] Lady of the Right View: Then stay wrongful. / Nights when heaven kneels on a mountain… are not so common. / Kneel. / All the way.
[13] ¶ Cloud covers the ridge. What happens under it is not for the song. By the time the cloud thins, neither of them is kneeling, and neither of them has let go.
[14] ¶ He holds her with one arm. The other is cloud. The ridge is still a mountain; the mountain is still a woman. She does not look up. She does not have to.
[15] ¶ By morning the ridge remembers two gods who would not let go. From that heat come eggs, and from the eggs, kings.
[16] ¶ Their eggs fall to earth on a hill called Guji, and wait for someone to sing.
[17] [CARD King Suro: King Suro. Born from a golden egg, and in no hurry to marry anyone local.]
[18] ── SCENE: Mount Guji ──
[19] ¶ On Earth, the people sing a song to call for a new king.
[20] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 2, Wonder 2 — King Suro / Turtle Song; Ha & Mintz tr., p. 158): Turtle, turtle — show your head. If you do not, we will roast and eat you.❞
[21] ¶ The people dig where the song tells them and find a box of six eggs, gold as the sun. Six babies hatch. The first one out is Suro. Each of the six founds a harbour kingdom:
[22] The Herald: …Eggs, you said?
[23] A villager: Six. In a box. From the sky.
[24] ¶ Nobody in Samhan finds this remarkable. Silla’s founder came out of an egg. Goguryeo’s founder came out of an egg. Here are six more. At some point one has to ask what the birds were doing.
[25] ¶ Gaya doesn’t have a crown. It has a league of iron harbours, six of them, give or take. No one king can lock the vote. Surabol would find that exhausting.
[26] [DIAGRAM gaya-league Gaya Confederacy · 가야 — Not one crown — a league of iron harbours.]
[27] [PLACE geumgwan: The harbour that sells iron to everyone, enemies included.]
[28] ── SCENE: The Red Sail ──
[29] ¶ **Queen Heo**, an Indian princess, becomes the first queen of Golden Gaya.
[30] [CARD Queen Heo: Heo Hwang-ok. She sailed farther than anyone in Samhan had heard of, and arrived dressed for it.]
[31] ¶ She arrives on a red-sailed ship at twenty-one — foreign, luminous, built like nowhere on this coast. The beach is only a door. The first time **Suro** falls in love is not on the sand.
[32] ¶ In the timber court of Golden Gaya she presents herself — no servant speaking for her, her own name, silk that does not belong to this hall. He is already on the dais. He meant to receive a princess. He receives a woman, and love hits him before protocol can stand up.
[33] ¶ Protocol is still trying to stand. He is already off the dais. He comes down with one arm — gold around violet, the same hold the sky used on the ridge, only this time the hall has columns and a floor.
[34] ¶ Servants had been sent to the ship. She refused them. So the court is where they meet — and the moment he sees her, speech leaves him like heat from an open kiln.
[35] Queen Heo: Have you come to fetch me… / or have you already begun to take me. / With your eyes. / Your mouth… looks dry.
[36] King Suro: … / ……You. / Your mouth…
[37] Queen Heo: Yes. / My mouth. / When the king looks at me like that… I get warmer. / Your hands… where do you mean to put them. / Even if you can’t speak — your hands know.
[38] King Suro: Your waist… / I mustn’t… / If I touch…
[39] Queen Heo: Then touch. / Since the king can’t choose… I’ll choose for you. / Here. / And here. / You’re shaking.
[40] King Suro: …Hungry… / I can’t… speak…
[41] Queen Heo: Then don’t speak. / If you’re hungry… take me first. / Slowly. / Not like a king — like a man.
[42] ¶ He makes a sound that is nowhere near a word, and she smiles as if it were the only answer she came across the sea for.
[43] ¶ On the hill she offers her silk trousers to the mountain spirit. He watches as if the rite were meant for him alone — jaw tight, hands useless at his sides.
[44] King Suro: …How will we know the mountain accepted it?
[45] Queen Heo: I can tell from the king’s eyes. / You look like someone who has already received.
[46] King Suro: …It is not I who received. / …I am going mad wanting to.
[47] Queen Heo: This country. / And by tonight… its king.
[48] ── SCENE: The Tent by the Water ──
[49] ¶ Two nights in a tent by the water before anyone may say marriage. By the second dusk he can barely keep his voice steady when she says his name — and she says it into his mouth so he has to swallow it.
[50] ¶ She turns so he can see the curve of her hip catching lamp, and he is kissing the throat he will marry before he has permission to call it a country.
[51] ¶ When he turns to the lamp she looks at the width of his back — muscle under purple-gold silk, a king’s body that the court never sees — and does not hide how that look sits on her mouth.
[52] Queen Heo: Slowly. / Your tongue — here. / The way you say my name. / The lower lip. / Below that. / More.
[53] King Suro: …At this rate I will learn the language. / Or I won’t. / I think I will fall apart first. / Inside you…
[54] Queen Heo: Then fall. / That way I have to put you back together every night. / With hands. / With mouth. / Until the king is a king again.
[55] ¶ The lamp burns low. She has taught him a dozen words since the dais, and in the dark she teaches him the rest without any — her hand on his wrist, showing him where, laughing when he is slow, then not laughing at all. She is twenty-one and crossed a sea with a stone pagoda in her ship’s hold to stop the waves; he is a king who hatched from an egg and has never once been told how. Neither of them is a god tonight. They are clumsy and greedy, and by the second hour they are good at it.
[56] King Suro: Say it— say it again— / In your Ayuta tongue— my name— / …I have forgotten what my own country is called—
[57] Queen Heo: My king— more— / Haa— my country has no word for this either— / Not yet— don’t go—
[58] ¶ The second night she is on top, violet silk off her shoulders and the gold tiger-pins still in her hair, because she refuses to take them out for a man who cannot yet say _good morning_ in her language. He loses his own words again. She keeps hers. When she comes apart she says something in the tongue of Ayuta that nobody on this coast will ever translate, and he decides it was his name.
[59] Queen Heo: My king’s— ah— / Stay— just like that—
[60] King Suro: …Wife. It is morning. / I cannot… take my hands away.
[61] Queen Heo: I know. / But I have not yet learned this country’s hours.
[62] King Suro: …The ministers are outside. / Before I go in… once more.
[63] Queen Heo: Once? / What a modest king.
[64] King Suro: I am not modest. / …I am only holding on. / Barely.
[65] Queen Heo: It does now. / I brought it with me — that sound, that night.
[66] ¶ They are married a hundred and fifty years — the record is firm about this and entirely untroubled by it — and have ten sons. She asks that two of them carry her name instead of his. He agrees without an argument, which in the whole of this history is the single strangest thing any king does.
[67] [WEDDING Queen Heo + King Suro]
[68] Queen Heo: My country is gone. Only the name is left.
[69] King Suro: Then we keep the name. I can always make another country.
[70] ¶ She dies at a hundred and fifty-seven. He follows ten years later and asks to be laid where he can see her hill.
[71] ¶ Her sons have her eyes, the colour of the far side of the sea. Gaya will marry into Silla and lose almost everything else. The eyes keep turning up anyway, a generation here and there, like a word nobody can quite translate.
[72] ══ DAY: DAY 2 ══
[73] ¶ Back on the Radiance road, the second morning comes up grey. Nine days of grain behind the palace gate. Bidam sends a runner across the field with a folded note. It says one word: tea.
[74] ¶ **Nine days of grain. One folded note. Will the Marshal of Silla come to tea with a traitor…?**
